title: MA8-13733
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXXX XXXXX, a 32-year old, married/separated, Tamil Sri Lankan male, claims refugee protection in Canada pursuant to Sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA)1.
The claimant alleges a well-founded fear of persecution by the army in Sri Lanka on the Convention grounds of race, religion, nationality and political opinion.

The claimant alleges that his is a XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, in Northern Sri Lanka. He claims that from as early as XXXXX 2000 he was persecuted by members of the Sri Lankan military because he is of Tamil Hindu origin living in the North.

In XXXXX 2006, the claimant alleges that he was forced by the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) to XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX in his XXXXX. He claims that in XXXXX the same year, the military accused him of helping the LTTE.

He fled to Colombo in XXXXX 2006 and was arrested and beaten by police. Following the expulsion of 500 Tamils from Colombo in June 2007, and with the help of an agent, he claims that he left Sri Lanka on XXXXX 2007.

He arrived in Canada using fraudulent documents on July 1st, 2007 and filed a claim for refugee protection on the same day. He was detained for identity documents and clarification of his itinerary coming to Canada.

The panel determines that the claimant is not a "Convention refugee" pursuant to Section 96 of Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA). The panel determines that the claimant is not a "person in need of protection" under Section 97(1) of the Act. ANALYSIS Identity

The panel is satisfied that the claimant is a Tamil male from northern Sri Lanka based upon his testimony in Sri Lankan Tamil and by his birth certificate and national identity card filed in the record2. Determinative Issue(s)
The determinative issue is whether the claimant's fear of persecution is objectively well-founded today and credibility. Credibility

The claimant submitted two amendments to his Personal Information Form (PIF). The first amendment, received August 2, 2010 contained updated information regarding his marital status (Question 3), relatives who had claimed refugee status (Question 5), his arrest by police (Question 9b), and his residence addresses (Question 11). The second amendment, received August 13, 2010, contained another update to Question 11, showing a four-month stay in Paris, France before coming to Canada. This document also included an updated itinerary (Question 21) which also showed his route via Paris, and it contained a one-sentence amendment for Question 31 in which he wrote that he fled Sri Lanka on XXXXX, 2007 with the help of an agent, and arrived in Canada on July 1, 2007.

In spite of these amendments, for the first half hour or more of his testimony the claimant still testified that he was in Sri Lanka from the XXXXX month, XXXXX 2006, until the XXXXX month, XXXXX 2007. After repeated questions to obtain clarification, the claimant said he lied upon arrival because he feared the agent who had told him not to say he was in France. He then confirmed he left Sri Lanka on XXXXX, 2007 and arrived in Canada on July 1, 2007. The claimant was then asked why he now admitted to going to Paris, France, when during his Port-of-Entry interview and detention hearings3 he had maintained that he had never gone to Paris. He said that about seven or eight months after he was in Canada and had submitted his PIF, he felt bad about lying and told his lawyer. The panel notes that he would have felt bad around March 2008, but notes his PIF amendment was made only in August 2010 even though he was represented by the same counsel at the time he completed his PIF on July 27, 2007. Counsel for the claimant offered that the amendment was a last minute change as he had only noticed the omission of France. That may be, but the fact remains that even at the hearing, the claimant's testimony was confused and evasive as to when he left Sri Lanka.

The claimant was then asked why he spent four months in France in 2007. He answered that the agent told him to wait and kept him there in a house with other French nationals. He said he stayed in the house the whole time and had little contact with the people in the house. Asked why he did not claim in France, he first said his motive was to come to Canada as Canada accepts refugees and then he said he was not afraid for his life in France. While the panel may accept that his agent told him to wait, the panel still finds that someone with a genuine fear for their life would claim refugee protection at the earliest available opportunity. The fact that the claimant denied being in Paris at the port-of-entry and was reticent to clearly explain his departure and his itinerary at the hearing, combined with the fact that he spent four months in Paris without claiming protection undermines his credibility with respect to his subjective fear in the mind of the panel. Section 96
The claimant was asked whom he feared today if returned to Sri Lanka today. The claimant answered that he feared the Sri Lankan army, the police and the EPDP group working with the army.

When asked why he feared the army, he testified that it was because the army had assaulted him on one occasion in XXXXX 2006 and they accused him of helping XXXXX XXXXX for the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE). He said the army had slapped his wife and child and had pushed the claimant. He claims this incident scared him and made him decide to flee his home and go to Colombo in order to leave the country. When asked if this was the only incident he experienced, he said yes. When asked if the military had come looking for him at his home in XXXXX since he left in XXXXX 2006, he said no. The panel finds that there is not more than a mere chance that he would be persecuted by the army today if returned to Sri Lanka given that they have not been looking for the claimant for over three years.

When asked why he feared the police, he said it was because he had been arrested in XXXXX 2006 in Colombo. He claims he was held for three days and beaten because they suspected him of LTTE involvement. He said he was released when his mother paid a bribe. Asked if there were any conditions given upon his release, he said they gave him the document deposed at Exhibit P-4, a copy of the receipt of arrest. The panel notes that this document indicates that the reason for his arrest was "failure to give reasons". Asked if he had registered in Colombo upon arrival and he said he did not. Asked why not, he said it was because only those staying in lodges had to register. The panel notes from Exhibit A-1, at Tab 13.5, a response to information request concerning the treatment of Tamils in Colombo, that as of June 2006, all Tamils living in the capital and its suburbs were required to register regardless of where or how long they were staying4. The panel also notes from several sources in the National Documentation Package on Sri Lanka that between 2006 and the end of the conflict in 2009, many Tamils in the Colombo area were routinely stopped and asked their purpose for being there as the authorities were looking for LTTE members, and that sometimes they were detained and beaten.

When asked if he had any other problems with the police between his one arrest in XXXXX 2006 and the end of XXXXX 2007 when he left the country, he said no. When asked if the police have been looking for him since his departure from the country, he again said no. Asked if there was a warrant for his arrest, he said no because he had never committed any crime. Given that the claimant was released without condition even though he had failed to register, and by his own testimony, there was only incident and no police have come looking for him since, the panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant was not of particular interest to the police when he left the country and that he does not face more than a mere chance of persecution by the police today.

The claimant alleged a fear of members of the EPDP whom he claims are working with the military. Asked if the EPDP had ever looked for him, he said no. Asked why he feared them, he said it was because he was a Tamil male and this Tamil group helps the military. When pressed as to why the EPDP would be after him he was unable to answer. The claimant failed to provide the panel with any details as to why this group would want to harm the claimant. The panel finds that he would not face more than a mere possibility of persecution by this group if he returned.

Deposed as Exhibit P-9 were three death certificates. Asked at the hearing who these people were, the claimant said they were family and distant family that had been killed in Sri Lanka. Asked if he knew the circumstances of their death, the claimant had difficulty giving any details. He identified one as a XXXXX (the term XXXXX is indicated on the death certificate). Asked if he was a XXXXX, he said no, the man XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX. For another, he said the man was working XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX but was unable to give details. For the third, he said it happened after he left the country and was unable to give details. Asked why these documents were deposed, he said because he is afraid that he too will be killed. The panel notes from the translated copies that two were killed in 2006 and the third was killed in late 2007. The panel is mindful that, unfortunately, many innocent people were killed during the 30 year civil war and that the violence escalated in the last few years leading up the end in May 2009; particularly in the North and the East of the country where these three people died. However, there was no evidence before the panel to suggest that these deaths were in any way linked to the particular situation of the claimant.

The claimant was asked if he was in touch with his family in Sri Lanka today. He said he speaks to his mother at least every two weeks. When asked by the panel what she says about the situation in Jaffna now, the claimant first said his mother told him it was worse. When asked to explain, the claimant was unable to give details or examples. He then said the EPDP is now even more powerful than before. When asked to explain, again he was unable to provide specific details but added that they were elected in the last elections. He also said that young boys were particularly afraid as old men had no problems. Asked to clarify what he meant, he conceded that he did not know the situation now and that he no longer asks his mother. Finally he said nothing is happening now but people are scared. In the absence of clear and convincing evidence that the situation is worse, the panel does not believe the claimant would be at risk if he returned.

A recent UNHCR report5 published July 5, 2010, states, "[g]iven the cessation of hostilities, Sri Lankans originating from the north of the country are no longer in need of international protection under broader refugee criteria or complementary forms of protection solely on the basis of risk of indiscriminate harm. In light of the improved human rights and security situation in Sri Lanka, there is no longer a need for group-based protection mechanisms or for a presumption of eligibility for Sri Lankans of Tamil ethnicity originating from the north of the country".

Although the same document cites that some young Tamil men from the North may be disproportionately subject to closer scrutiny if they had suspected LTTE links, the panel finds that the claimant has failed to meet his burden of proof to establish that he would face a reasonable chance of persecution on a Convention ground if returned today. Section 97(1)(a)

The Federal Court has held that pursuant to IRPA Section 97(1): (i) there must be persuasive evidence (i.e., balance of probabilities) establishing the facts on which a claimant relies to say that he or she faces a substantial danger of being tortured or of having cruel and unusual treatment or punishment inflicted upon his or her return; and (ii) the danger or risk must be such that it is more likely than not that he or she would be tortured or subjected to other cruel and other degrading treatments6.

In the absence of any evidence to suggest he would face any danger, believed on substantial grounds to exist, of torture within the meaning of Article 1 of the "Convention Against Torture", the panel finds that this ground is not open to the claimant. Section 97(1)(b)

The panel then considered whether the claimant is a person who faces a risk to life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment. However, given that there are no reasons, other than those analyzed under Section 96, before the panel to support his claim under this section of IRPA, the panel finds that this ground is not open to the claimant.

Based on the totality of the evidence before it, the panel finds there is not a serious possibility that the claimant would be persecuted for any Convention ground, if he was to return to Sri Lanka today. Nor does the panel find the claimant is a person in need of protection under Section 97 (1). For the reasons cited herein, the panel rejects the claim.
